h: A Mansion, a Marsh and a Miniature Railway
p: Port Lympne has a fascinating history alongside its animals. At the heart of the estate is a grand mansion built in the early twentieth century for Sir Philip Sassoon, a politician and art collector who entertained the great and the good of the day there, with Winston Churchill among his guests. The house is famous for its Tent Room, painted by the artist Rex Whistler, and the terraced gardens drop down the hillside with views over Romney Marsh.

Practicalities first: the site is huge and hilly, so give yourselves a full day and wear comfortable shoes. The safari experience gets busy at peak times, so it's worth heading there earlier in the day. Bring a coat and snacks, as you'll be covering plenty of ground, and keep the camera or phone charged up, because there are photo opportunities around every corner.

Hythe is a great base for exploring. The Romney, Hythe and Dymchurch Railway, a miniature steam line, runs from Hythe across the marsh all the way to Dungeness, a strange and wonderful shingle headland with lighthouses, fishing boats and a nature reserve. In Hythe itself, St Leonard's Church has a crypt that holds a large collection of human skulls and bones, an unusual and slightly spooky stop for older kids. Brockhill Country Park, just outside town, has a lake, woodland walks and play areas for little ones. Folkestone, a short drive east, has a lively harbour arm, sandy Sunny Sands beach and the Leas, a clifftop promenade with sea views across the Channel.
